es: Detectar pistas de que un narrador no es fiable, leer entre líneas y deducir qué pasó realmente con must have, can't have y might have.

vocabulary.es: interesado, que favorece al propio narrador

teaching.en: An unreliable narrator is not always a liar; he may simply misjudge events, forget details or conceal what he is ashamed of.
teaching.es: Un narrador poco fiable no siempre es un mentiroso; puede simplemente juzgar mal los hechos, olvidar detalles u ocultar aquello de lo que se avergüenza.
teaching.explanationEs: Poco fiable no significa mentiroso: el narrador puede equivocarse o callar sin mala intención.
segments: An unreliable narrator is not always a liar; he may simply
misjudge events, forget details or conceal what he is ashamed of.
teaching.audioText: An unreliable narrator is not always a liar; he may simply misjudge events, forget details or conceal what he is ashamed of.

teaching.en: A single clue, such as a date or a muddy boot, can cast doubt on the narrator's version of events.
teaching.es: Una sola pista, como una fecha o una bota embarrada, puede poner en duda la versión de los hechos del narrador.
teaching.explanationEs: Cast doubt on + algo: una pista sembrada en el texto debilita lo que se cuenta.
segments: A single clue, such as a date or a muddy
boot, can cast doubt on the narrator's version of events.
teaching.audioText: A single clue, such as a date or a muddy boot, can cast doubt on the narrator's version of events.

teaching.en: When a story feels suspicious, read between the lines: what a narrator leaves out matters as much as what he says.
teaching.es: Cuando una historia resulta sospechosa, lee entre líneas: lo que el narrador omite importa tanto como lo que dice.
teaching.explanationEs: Suspicious describe lo que hace dudar; leer entre líneas es fijarse en lo no dicho.
segments: When a story feels suspicious, read between the lines: what a
narrator leaves out matters as much as what he says.
teaching.audioText: When a story feels suspicious, read between the lines: what a narrator leaves out matters as much as what he says.

teaching.en: He will claim he stayed in, but mud on his boots means he must have been out after dark.
teaching.es: Afirmará que se quedó en casa, pero el barro de sus botas indica que tuvo que salir después de anochecer.
teaching.explanationEs: Must have + participio: deducción casi segura sobre el pasado, apoyada en una pista.
segments: He will claim he stayed in, but mud on his
boots means he must have been out after dark.
teaching.audioText: He will claim he stayed in, but mud on his boots means he must have been out after dark.

teaching.en: A self-serving narrator may exaggerate his courage and gloss over his mistakes, so the storm might have been milder.
teaching.es: Un narrador interesado puede exagerar su valentía y quitar importancia a sus errores, así que la tormenta pudo haber sido más suave.
teaching.explanationEs: Might have + participio: posibilidad sin certeza. Gloss over: tratar un fallo como si no importara.
segments: A self-serving narrator may exaggerate his courage and gloss over
his mistakes, so the storm might have been milder.
teaching.audioText: A self-serving narrator may exaggerate his courage and gloss over his mistakes, so the storm might have been milder.

teaching.en: If two witnesses contradict each other, one of them can't have remembered events accurately, so the reader must weigh both.
teaching.es: Si dos testigos se contradicen, uno de ellos no puede haber recordado los hechos con exactitud, así que el lector debe sopesar ambos.
teaching.explanationEs: Can't have + participio: casi seguro que no ocurrió. Para deducir no se usa mustn't have.
segments: If two witnesses contradict each other, one of them can't
have remembered events accurately, so the reader must weigh both.
teaching.audioText: If two witnesses contradict each other, one of them can't have remembered events accurately, so the reader must weigh both.

prompt.es: Elige la deducción más sólida a partir de la pista del texto.

choices.text: He can't have been outside, because he was reading all night.
He can't have been at the library, so the coat must belong to someone else.
He must have been outside at some point that evening.

feedback.es: Un abrigo que huele a lluvia apoya una deducción con must have; la segunda se fía de la versión del narrador y la tercera inventa un dato que el texto no da.

hint.es: Busca la opción que se apoya en el olor a lluvia del abrigo.

origin.text: «I spent the whole evening at home with a book,» the narrator insists. Yet the next page mentions that the library had closed at eight and that his coat smelled of rain.

prompt.es: Completa: «Así que no puede haber estado dormido.»

feedback.es: Si alguien oyó su auto a medianoche, dormir es casi imposible: la deducción negativa se hace con can't have.

hint.es: Deducción negativa sobre el pasado: no uses mustn't.

origin.text: The narrator says he was asleep by ten. The neighbour, however, heard his car at midnight. So he ___ have been asleep.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Puede que exagerara su valentía para quedar bien.»

answer.text: He might have exaggerated his courage to look good

feedback.es: Might have + participio plantea una posibilidad sobre el pasado; to look good expresa el motivo.

hint.es: Sujeto, might have, participio, y al final el motivo con to.

prompt.es: Relaciona cada detalle del relato con lo que sugiere.

pairs: He describes every hour of the day except the one after dinner.

pairs.es: Pasa por alto justo lo que podría comprometerle.

pairs: Three neighbours call it a small fire; he says it ruined the house.
He says, without being asked, that he has nothing to hide.

pairs.es: Su defensa no pedida resulta sospechosa.

pairs: His diary says he was ill, but a friend's letter says he was at the party.

feedback.es: Cada detalle apunta a un tipo distinto de no fiabilidad: omisión, exageración, defensa excesiva y contradicción.

pairs: He describes every hour of the day except the one after dinner.

pairs.es: Pasa por alto justo lo que podría comprometerle.

pairs: Three neighbours call it a small fire; he says it ruined the house.
He says, without being asked, that he has nothing to hide.

pairs.es: Su defensa no pedida resulta sospechosa.

pairs: His diary says he was ill, but a friend's letter says he was at the party.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige qué concluye la hablante sobre Tom.

choices.text: The way he repeats himself makes her doubt him.
Saying the same thing so often proves that he is guilty.
She still believes him, despite the receipt and his refusal to look at her.

feedback.es: La hablante suma las negativas repetidas y el recibo del día anterior y duda de Tom; no afirma que esté probado que es culpable ni que aún le crea.

origin.audio: I wanted to believe Tom. He told the police, three times, that he had never met the victim, and he never once looked at me. But a receipt from her shop was in his coat, dated the day before. A man with nothing to hide does not repeat himself like that.

prompt.es: Completa: «Una sola fecha puede poner en duda la historia del narrador.»

feedback.es: Cast doubt on es la colocación habitual para poner algo en duda con un dato concreto.

origin.text: The narrator gives every detail of the evening except the time he returned. One date in the letter can ___ doubt on his whole version of events.

prompt.es: ¿Qué dato del texto contradice con más fuerza a Carlos?

choices.text: He was the first person to ask about the deadline.
His signature was still wet on the last page.
He phoned the lawyer twice that week.

feedback.es: La firma fresca es una prueba material de que firmó el documento que niega haber visto; preguntar por el plazo o llamar dos veces al abogado solo sugiere interés.

origin.text: Carlos tells the court that he never saw the contract. «I would have remembered it,» he says, folding his arms and looking at the floor. Later, Sara remarks that he was the first person to ask about the deadline, that he phoned the lawyer twice that week, and that his signature was still wet on the last page of the document.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige qué sugiere la hablante sobre la narradora de la novela.

choices.text: She dislikes her brother and has hidden it from readers.
She was treated unfairly by her mother, as she herself believes.
She may have caused an argument but avoids saying so.

feedback.es: La narradora omite justo el momento clave y el enojo de su madre; el lector deduce que ella pudo ser la causa, no que fuera tratada con injusticia.

origin.audio: In the third chapter, the narrator describes her brother's wedding in loving detail: the flowers, the music, the speeches. She mentions, almost in passing, that she left before the cake was cut, and that her mother did not speak to her for a month afterwards. She never explains why. Readers who accept her warm tone at face value will miss the gap. Because the most important moment of the whole day is the one she skips, we are invited to suspect that her own behaviour was the reason for the silence.

prompt.es: Completa: «Los autores pasan por alto la cifra en una sola frase.»

feedback.es: Gloss over describe tratar un dato incómodo con prisa, para que no llame la atención.

origin.text: The report praises the scheme at length. The one figure that looks bad appears only in the last paragraph, where the authors ___ over it in a single sentence.

prompt.es: Escribe dos deducciones sobre el narrador: una con must have, otra con might have.

answer.text: He must have entered the house earlier than he says, because he had the keys in his hand. He might have waited to conceal something.
accepted: He must have entered the house earlier than he says, because he had the keys in his hand. He might have waited to conceal something.
He must have lied about the door, because he still had the keys. He could have concealed the truth for three hours.

feedback.es: Una buena respuesta apoya must have en una pista (las llaves o la demora) y deja might o could have para una posibilidad.

origin.text: Un narrador dice que encontró la puerta abierta y llamó a la policía de inmediato, pero el informe dice que llamó tres horas después y que tenía las llaves en la mano. Escribe dos frases: una con must have y otra con might have.

prompt.es: ¿Qué deja entrever la respuesta de Leo al agente?

choices.text: That he is nervous about one hour and wants to steer attention away.
That he has a poor memory and cannot be blamed for the gaps.
That he finds the question funny and is making fun of the officer.

feedback.es: Dice que su memoria es vaga, pero relata todo con detalle salvo una hora: la vaguedad parece una excusa para evitar esa hora, no una burla ni un olvido real.

origin.text: When the police officer asked where he had been on Friday, Leo laughed and said, «Honestly, I could tell you every minute, but my memory is a little vague.» Then he described his Friday in great detail, from breakfast to the late film, apart from the hour between nine and ten, which he never mentioned again.

prompt.es: Ordena: «No puede haber leído la carta antes de escribir su respuesta.»

answer.text: She can't have read the letter before she wrote her reply

feedback.es: Can't have + participio niega con casi certeza un hecho pasado; before introduce el momento.

prompt.es: Completa: «Tom afirma que pasó el viernes en el cine.»

feedback.es: Claim presenta lo que dice el personaje como algo dudoso, justo antes del dato que lo contradice.

origin.text: Tom ___ that he spent Friday at the cinema. However, the receipt in his pocket is from a garage.

es: Usar con precisión el vocabulario de análisis literario (recurring motif, symbol, foreshadowing, imagery, evoke, allude to, resonate) en una reseña crítica.

teaching.en: A recurring motif, such as a locked door, becomes a symbol once it stands for something the characters cannot face.
teaching.es: Un motivo recurrente, como una puerta cerrada con llave, se convierte en símbolo cuando representa algo que los personajes no pueden afrontar.
teaching.explanationEs: El motivo se repite; el símbolo representa una idea. Un mismo elemento puede ser las dos cosas.
segments: A recurring motif, such as a locked door, becomes a
symbol once it stands for something the characters cannot face.
teaching.audioText: A recurring motif, such as a locked door, becomes a symbol once it stands for something the characters cannot face.

teaching.en: Foreshadowing prepares the reader for what follows: a cracked mirror in chapter one may warn of the betrayal in chapter ten.
teaching.es: El presagio prepara al lector para lo que viene: un espejo roto en el primer capítulo puede avisar de la traición del décimo.
teaching.explanationEs: Foreshadowing anticipa sin decirlo abiertamente; se reconoce al releer.
segments: Foreshadowing prepares the reader for what follows: a cracked mirror in
chapter one may warn of the betrayal in chapter ten.
teaching.audioText: Foreshadowing prepares the reader for what follows: a cracked mirror in chapter one may warn of the betrayal in chapter ten.

teaching.en: The imagery of fog and wet stone can evoke a deep sense of loneliness without the narrator ever naming the feeling.
teaching.es: Las imágenes de niebla y piedra mojada pueden evocar una profunda sensación de soledad sin que el narrador nombre nunca el sentimiento.
teaching.explanationEs: Imagery son las imágenes sensoriales; evoke indica que despiertan una emoción.
segments: The imagery of fog and wet stone can evoke a deep
sense of loneliness without the narrator ever naming the feeling.
teaching.audioText: The imagery of fog and wet stone can evoke a deep sense of loneliness without the narrator ever naming the feeling.

teaching.en: A subtle writer will allude to a scandal rather than describe it, leaving the reader to supply the missing details.
teaching.es: Un escritor sutil aludirá a un escándalo en lugar de describirlo, y dejará que el lector complete los detalles que faltan.
teaching.explanationEs: Allude to + algo: mencionarlo de pasada, sin desarrollarlo.
segments: A subtle writer will allude to a scandal rather than
describe it, leaving the reader to supply the missing details.
teaching.audioText: A subtle writer will allude to a scandal rather than describe it, leaving the reader to supply the missing details.

teaching.en: A novelist can convey a central theme without stating it, which is why many endings are open to interpretation.
teaching.es: Un novelista puede transmitir un tema central sin enunciarlo, y por eso muchos finales están abiertos a la interpretación.
teaching.explanationEs: Open to interpretation: admite más de una lectura razonable.
segments: A novelist can convey a central theme without stating it,
which is why many endings are open to interpretation.
teaching.audioText: A novelist can convey a central theme without stating it, which is why many endings are open to interpretation.

teaching.en: A heavy-handed symbol explains itself too loudly, whereas a good story can resonate with readers long after the last page.
teaching.es: Un símbolo pesado se explica a sí mismo con demasiado ruido, mientras que una buena historia puede calar en los lectores mucho después de la última página.
teaching.explanationEs: Resonate with + personas. Heavy-handed es una crítica: falta sutileza.
segments: A heavy-handed symbol explains itself too loudly, whereas a good
story can resonate with readers long after the last page.
teaching.audioText: A heavy-handed symbol explains itself too loudly, whereas a good story can resonate with readers long after the last page.

prompt.es: ¿Qué término describe el elemento que reaparece en el texto?

choices.text: A recurring motif whose appearances warn of trouble.
A central theme that the narrator states openly.
A piece of imagery that has no link to the plot.

feedback.es: Un objeto que vuelve a aparecer y anuncia problemas es un motivo recurrente con función de presagio; no es un tema ni una imagen suelta.

hint.es: Piensa en algo que se repite y, además, avisa de lo que viene.

origin.text: In chapter one, a red umbrella is left by the river. It returns in chapters four and nine, each time just before something goes wrong for the family.

prompt.es: Completa: «El faro se convierte en un símbolo de esperanza.»

feedback.es: Una cosa concreta que representa una idea, como la esperanza, es un símbolo.

hint.es: Es una cosa concreta que representa una idea abstracta.

origin.text: The writer never says that the lighthouse means anything. Yet every time it appears, the characters look up, and it becomes a ___ of hope.

prompt.es: Ordena: «La autora solo alude al escándalo en una frase.»

answer.text: The writer only alludes to the scandal in one line

feedback.es: Allude to + algo: se menciona de pasada, sin describirlo, que es justo lo sutil.

hint.es: Tras alludes va to, y después lo que se menciona.

prompt.es: Relaciona cada recurso con lo que hace en el texto.

pairs: a recurring motif

pairs.es: Reaparece a lo largo de la obra.

pairs: a heavy-handed symbol
subtle foreshadowing

pairs.es: Avisa de lo que vendrá sin decirlo.

pairs: vivid imagery

pairs.es: Despierta una emoción con detalles sensoriales.

feedback.es: Cada recurso cumple una función distinta: repetir, representar con insistencia, anticipar con sutileza o despertar emociones.

pairs: a recurring motif

pairs.es: Reaparece a lo largo de la obra.

pairs: a heavy-handed symbol
subtle foreshadowing

pairs.es: Avisa de lo que vendrá sin decirlo.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige por qué la hablante lo llama motivo y no símbolo.

choices.text: It is tied to departures, so it plainly stands for the characters' fear of leaving.
It keeps returning, but what it stands for is not yet clear.
It repeats before every departure, so it works mainly as foreshadowing.

feedback.es: Un motivo se repite; para hablar de símbolo haría falta saber qué representa la ventana, y eso todavía no está claro. Que aparezca antes de cada partida no prueba su significado.

origin.audio: The director keeps returning to the same image: a window left open. Nobody comments on it, yet it appears before every departure. I would call it a motif, not a symbol, because it is not yet clear what the window stands for.

prompt.es: Completa: «Sus imágenes de ceniza y humo evocan una profunda sensación de pérdida.»

feedback.es: Evoke y convey describen el efecto emocional de las imágenes sobre el lector.

origin.text: The writer never states that the town is losing its people, and she never describes a single goodbye. Yet her imagery of smoke and dust ___ a deep sense of loss on every page.

prompt.es: Completa cuatro frases de la reseña con el término literario adecuado.

feedback.es: Lo que se repite pide motif, lo que anticipa pide foreshadows, mencionar de pasada pide alludes to y las imágenes sensoriales piden imagery.

sentences: The long road is a recurring ___ that returns in every chapter and links the characters' separate journeys.
A cracked mirror in chapter two ___ the betrayal that comes in chapter ten.
The author ___ to the family's money problems in a single line and then moves on.
The writer's ___ of wind and dry stone evokes a place that time has abandoned.
origin.text: Reviewers praise The Long Road for being quiet and gentle: the author never explains how the story is built, so readers must work out the pattern for themselves.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige qué actitud muestra la crítica hacia el faro de la novela.

choices.text: She believes the lighthouse would work better if it appeared more often.
She considers the ending weak because the lighthouse is never explained.
She feels the writer leaves too little for the reader to work out.

feedback.es: Critica que el símbolo se repita y se explique tanto que no deja trabajo al lector: es una crítica a la falta de sutileza, no a que aparezca poco ni a un final sin resolver.

origin.audio: I wanted to like the new novel. The lighthouse appears on the first page, and on the second, and on the third, each time described as lonely, patient and faithful. By chapter six the writer has practically written in the margin that it is a symbol of hope. A reader deserves a little more trust. If she had mentioned the lighthouse only twice, I think I would have felt its meaning for myself, and the ending might have resonated far more. As it is, I closed the book feeling that I had been told what to think, page after page, and that is not what I read novels for.

prompt.es: Completa: «El director lo transmite mediante silencios y frases sin terminar.»

feedback.es: Convey es el verbo natural para lo que un autor transmite al lector sin decirlo abiertamente.

origin.text: The film never tells us that the relationship is failing. The director ___ it through long silences and broken sentences.

prompt.es: Escribe dos frases de reseña: a symbol of y resonate with.

answer.text: The broken bridge is a symbol of the family's lost trust. The final scene will resonate with anyone who has ever said goodbye.
accepted: The broken bridge is a symbol of the family's lost trust. The final scene will resonate with anyone who has ever said goodbye.
The broken bridge is a symbol of the trust that the family has lost. The ending resonates with many readers who have lost someone.

feedback.es: Una buena reseña nombra el símbolo con a symbol of y valora su efecto con resonate with.

origin.text: Reseña de una novela: un puente roto simboliza la confianza perdida de una familia, y el final conmoverá a cualquiera que se haya despedido de alguien. Escribe dos frases: una con a symbol of y otra con resonate with.

prompt.es: ¿Qué sugiere el texto sobre el paraguas rojo de la película?

choices.text: Its meaning is left open, so viewers can read it differently.
It is a motif the director uses to foreshadow the final scene.
It is an obvious symbol that some viewers find too heavy-handed.

feedback.es: El director no lo explica y el público duda entre pérdida y liberación: el final está abierto a interpretación.

origin.text: The director never explains the red umbrella that appears in every scene, and when the film ends with it drifting out of frame, the audience is left to decide whether it marks a loss or a release. Some viewers left the cinema annoyed and talking loudly about the price of the ticket; others stayed in their seats for a long time, silent.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Sus imágenes pesadas estropean una novela por lo demás sutil.»

answer.text: Her heavy-handed imagery spoils an otherwise subtle novel

feedback.es: Heavy-handed critica la falta de sutileza, y otherwise subtle marca el contraste con el resto de la novela.

prompt.es: Completa: «El final está abierto a interpretación.»

feedback.es: Open to interpretation es la colocación para un final que admite lecturas distintas.

origin.text: The two readers disagree about the last page. The ending is ___ to interpretation on purpose, and the author refuses to say what she meant.

title.en: Characters, plot and point of view
title.es: Personajes, trama y punto de vista

es: Identificar punto de vista, motivación, tema, tono e inferencia en un fragmento de relato, respondiendo con pruebas del texto.

teaching.en: The protagonist narrates her own story, so the narrative viewpoint is limited to what she notices, understands and chooses to tell.
teaching.es: La protagonista narra su propia historia, así que el punto de vista narrativo se limita a lo que ella observa, entiende y decide contar.
teaching.explanationEs: En primera persona solo vemos lo que el narrador ve: por eso su punto de vista es limitado.
segments: The protagonist narrates her own story, so the narrative viewpoint is
limited to what she notices, understands and chooses to tell.
teaching.audioText: The protagonist narrates her own story, so the narrative viewpoint is limited to what she notices, understands and chooses to tell.

teaching.en: The plot may show a woman chasing a promotion, but her underlying motivation is a need to prove her father wrong.
teaching.es: La trama puede mostrar a una mujer que persigue un ascenso, pero su motivación de fondo es la necesidad de demostrar que su padre se equivocaba.
teaching.explanationEs: La trama es lo que ocurre; la motivación de fondo es lo que empuja al personaje, y rara vez se dice.
segments: The plot may show a woman chasing a promotion, but her
underlying motivation is a need to prove her father wrong.
teaching.audioText: The plot may show a woman chasing a promotion, but her underlying motivation is a need to prove her father wrong.

teaching.en: The tone of a passage is the attitude it carries: a detached tone can report a quarrel as if it were a weather forecast.
teaching.es: El tono de un pasaje es la actitud que transmite: un tono distante puede contar una discusión como si fuera un pronóstico del tiempo.
teaching.explanationEs: Tone se identifica con adjetivos (detached, bitter, tender) y se apoya con pruebas del texto.
segments: The tone of a passage is the attitude it carries: a detached
tone can report a quarrel as if it were a weather forecast.
teaching.audioText: The tone of a passage is the attitude it carries: a detached tone can report a quarrel as if it were a weather forecast.

teaching.en: A wry remark, such as calling a failed dinner a great success, shows amusement and disappointment at the same time.
teaching.es: Un comentario irónico, como llamar gran éxito a una cena fallida, muestra diversión y decepción a la vez.
teaching.explanationEs: Wry indica humor seco que suele esconder otro sentimiento.
segments: A wry remark, such as calling a failed dinner a
great success, shows amusement and disappointment at the same time.
teaching.audioText: A wry remark, such as calling a failed dinner a great success, shows amusement and disappointment at the same time.

teaching.en: To infer a feeling, watch what a character does: she may be reluctant to admit that she still misses him.
teaching.es: Para inferir un sentimiento, fíjate en lo que hace un personaje: puede ser reacia a admitir que todavía lo echa de menos.
teaching.explanationEs: Infer es deducir lo que el texto no dice con palabras; reluctant to admit + verbo.
segments: To infer a feeling, watch what a character does: she
may be reluctant to admit that she still misses him.
teaching.audioText: To infer a feeling, watch what a character does: she may be reluctant to admit that she still misses him.

teaching.en: In hindsight, her bitter comments about the wedding read as grief, and the betrayal she describes is perhaps her own.
teaching.es: Visto en retrospectiva, sus comentarios amargos sobre la boda se leen como duelo, y la traición que describe quizá sea la suya.
teaching.explanationEs: In hindsight: con lo que sabemos después. Bitter describe un tono resentido.
segments: In hindsight, her bitter comments about the wedding read as
grief, and the betrayal she describes is perhaps her own.
teaching.audioText: In hindsight, her bitter comments about the wedding read as grief, and the betrayal she describes is perhaps her own.

prompt.es: ¿Qué tono domina el fragmento sobre Mia y la carta?

choices.text: Openly angry from the very first line of the passage.
Gently funny, with some worry behind the jokes.
Calm and detached, like a short factual report.

feedback.es: El humor de «as if it might bite» da un tono ligero y divertido, con cierta tensión por debajo de la broma; no hay enojo abierto ni frialdad de informe.

hint.es: Fíjate en la última comparación: ¿es seria o divertida, y qué esconde?

origin.text: When the letter finally arrived, Mia left it on the kitchen table for three days. She dusted around it, watered the plants beside it and told her sister, twice, that it was probably nothing important. Then, one morning, she opened it with a pen, as if it might bite.

prompt.es: ¿Qué se puede inferir de la actitud de Mia ante la carta?

choices.text: She has forgotten that the letter is still on the table.
She already knows what it says and feels quite relieved about it.
She fears what the letter says but will not admit it.

feedback.es: Limpiar alrededor de la carta y repetir que no es importante delata miedo, aunque Mia no lo reconozca.

hint.es: Piensa en lo que hace durante tres días, no en lo que dice.

origin.text: When the letter finally arrived, Mia left it on the kitchen table for three days. She dusted around it, watered the plants beside it and told her sister, twice, that it was probably nothing important. Then, one morning, she opened it with a pen, as if it might bite.

prompt.es: Completa: «Mia es reacia a abrir la carta, aunque no lo admite.»

feedback.es: Reluctant describe a quien no quiere hacer algo aunque sepa que debe hacerlo.

hint.es: Adjetivo que significa «reacio» y va seguido de to.

origin.text: Mia keeps telling her sister that the letter is probably nothing. In truth, she is ___ to open it, although she will not admit it.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige el punto de vista y lo que revela el narrador.

choices.text: First person: the narrator tells a secret of his own.
First person: the narrator reports what his brother later told him.
First person: the narrator admits that he misjudged his brother.

feedback.es: El narrador dice «I have never told my brother» y cuenta su propio secreto en primera persona; no cita ninguna confesión del hermano ni reconoce haberse equivocado.

origin.audio: I have never told my brother that I read his letters home from abroad. He believed the envelopes had never been opened, and for forty years I let him believe it. Was it curiosity that made me do it, or was it the fear that he would write something about me? I still cannot say. What I can say is that his handwriting changed after the second year, and that I understood why before he did.

prompt.es: ¿Qué puede inferirse del último comentario del narrador sobre la letra?

choices.text: He suspected that his brother had noticed the opened envelopes.
He understood what was happening to his brother before the brother did.
He blames himself for having sent his brother abroad.

feedback.es: Si entendió el cambio de letra antes que su hermano, captó lo que le ocurría antes que él: es una inferencia, no algo que el texto afirme.

prompt.es: Relaciona cada frase con el tono que transmite.

pairs: «Oh, wonderful,» she said, looking at the flood in her kitchen.
He filed the report, closed the drawer and never mentioned her name again.
Every word of the toast was kind, and every word hurt a little.
She laughed at the joke, then went to wash her hands for ten minutes.

feedback.es: El tono se deduce de la actitud que dejan ver los detalles: ironía, frialdad, amargura o nerviosismo.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige qué sugiere el final del fragmento.

choices.text: She is relieved, since the piano had become a burden for her too.
She is proud of having kept the diary hidden for twenty years.
Her polite approval covers resentment and a private loss.

feedback.es: Dice que está encantada, pero repite «sensible» a solas: la ironía deja ver resentimiento y la pérdida de su escondite.

origin.audio: My sister called to tell me, in a bright voice, that she had finally sold our mother's piano. It was, she said, the sensible thing to do, since nobody played it any more. I told her I was very happy for her. She sounded pleased with herself, the way people do when a long argument is over. Then I put down the phone, went into the hall and looked for a long time at the empty space where the piano had been. Behind it, twenty years ago, I had hidden my first real diary. Sensible, I said aloud, to nobody. Very sensible.

prompt.es: ¿Qué tema sugiere el fragmento de la venta del piano?

choices.text: Practical choices can take away the place where a memory lives.
Sisters who argue over their mother's things rarely forgive each other.
Sentimental objects lose their value once nobody uses them.

feedback.es: La decisión «sensata» de la hermana borra el lugar donde la narradora guardaba su diario: el tema es el coste íntimo de lo práctico, no el reparto de bienes ni el valor de los objetos.

origin.text: I sold the house in June, and I told everybody that it was the right moment. My daughter said nothing. She simply went upstairs and took the clock from the hall, the one that had never kept the time. I pretended not to notice, and I went on talking about the price.

origin.audio: I went in expecting very little, and I came out a little embarrassed by how much I had enjoyed it. The script is predictable, the music is far too loud and the young lead is given lines that no one could say with a straight face. And yet I could not look away. prompt.es: Escribe una reseña con dos deducciones, un ejemplo, un defecto y una recomendación.

answer.text: The Quiet Harbour follows a woman who returns to her fishing village after ten years and finds that nobody wants to talk about the night her father disappeared. From the first scene, the film is gripping: the camera stays on faces, and every silence seems to hide something. The cast is excellent, and the young lead almost steals the show. Her brother must have known more than he admits, because he never looks at her during the wedding, and the old neighbour, who says she never left her house, can't have stayed in that night, since her boots were covered in mud. The dialogue is convincing, for example in the kitchen scene, where two sentences reveal a whole family history. The one flaw is the pacing: the final twist feels rushed, and the ending may fall short of the promise of the first hour. Even so, I would highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys a slow, thoughtful mystery.
accepted: The Quiet Harbour follows a woman who returns to her fishing village after ten years and finds that nobody wants to talk about the night her father disappeared. Her brother must have known more than he admits, because he never looks at her during the wedding, and the old neighbour, who says she never left her house, can't have stayed in that night, since her boots were covered in mud. The dialogue is convincing, for example in the kitchen scene, where two sentences reveal a whole family history. The one flaw is the pacing: the final twist feels rushed, and the ending may fall short of the promise of the first hour. Even so, I would highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys a slow, thoughtful mystery.

The Quiet Harbour is about a woman who goes back to her village by the sea after ten years. The film is stunning to look at and the actors are very good. Her brother must have hidden something from her, because he avoids her eyes at the wedding. The neighbour can't have stayed at home that night, since her boots were full of mud. The dialogue feels real, for instance in the kitchen scene, where a few words explain the whole family. The main weakness is that the story is predictable and the ending is rushed, so it falls short of its beginning. Nevertheless, I recommend it to everybody who likes slow films with a mystery, because the performances alone are worth the ticket.

es: Debatir una historia en un club de lectura: proponer una lectura, defenderla con dos deducciones, conceder un punto y discrepar con educación.

origin.audio: At the club, Carlos argued for an hour that the narrator was a liar. Sara listened, nodded at the right moments, and then said that he made a fair point about the letter, and that she would gladly concede it. What she could not accept, she said, was that one lie makes every page a lie. A reader who reads too much into one detail ends up writing a different novel. Carlos smiled, looked at the ceiling and suggested that they should agree to disagree, which, everyone understood, meant that he had not changed his mind either.

answer.text: I would argue that the ending of The Blue Door is ambiguous on purpose. The narrator says that nobody ever lived in the house, but he can't have been honest, because he also says that his sister left after an argument. The wet letter is a clue: she must have been upset when she wrote it, and he might have kept it hidden for years. A plausible reading is that the blue door is a symbol of a memory that he cannot close. Carlos argues that the narrator is simply lying to us, and I concede that this is possible. However, I take issue with the idea that one lie spoils the whole book, and I am not entirely convinced that the writer wants us to be certain. But we should not read too much into one lie. The imagery of cold and rain makes the sadness resonate, and the ending stays open to interpretation. We will have to agree to disagree, Carlos.
accepted: I would argue that the ending of The Blue Door is ambiguous on purpose. The narrator says that nobody ever lived in the house, but he can't have been honest, because he also says that his sister left after an argument. A plausible reading is that the blue door is a symbol of a memory that he cannot close. Carlos argues that the narrator is simply lying to us, and I concede that this is possible.
